chapter_summary:
Design space exploration is the process of systematically evaluating different architectural configurations to find the optimal design for a given set of constraints (performance, power, area, cost).

**The design space:**

The design space of a processor includes:
- Pipeline depth: 5–20 stages
- Issue width: 1–8 instructions per cycle
- Cache size: 8 KB–64 MB
- Cache associativity: 1–32 way
- Number of functional units: 2–20
- ROB size: 40–900 entries
- Branch predictor size: 1K–64K entries
- Memory bandwidth: 10–1000 GB/s

The total number of possible configurations is enormous (e.g., 10 parameters with 5 options each = 5^10 = 9,765,625 configurations). Evaluating all configurations is impossible, so architects use techniques to explore the space efficiently.

**Simulation:**

Architectural simulators are the primary tool for design space exploration. They model the processor at the cycle level and execute benchmark programs to measure performance.

- **SimpleScalar:** One of the earliest widely used simulators. Models a MIPS-like processor with configurable parameters.
- **Gem5:** The current standard for academic research. Models x86, ARM, and RISC-V processors with detailed cache, memory, and interconnect models. Supports full-system and syscall-emulation modes.
- **Sniper:** A faster simulator that uses interval modeling rather than cycle-by-cycle simulation. Good for exploring large design spaces.
- **ZSim:** Another fast simulator using parallel simulation techniques.
- **Marss-x86:** A detailed x86 simulator based on PTLSim.

**Simulation methodology:**
1. **Select benchmarks:** Use representative workloads (e.g., SPEC CPU, PARSEC, SPLASH-2).
2. **Select metrics:** Performance (IPC), power (watts), energy (joules), area (mm²).
3. **Configure simulator:** Set the parameters for the architecture being evaluated.
4. **Run simulations:** Execute the benchmarks and collect statistics.
5. **Analyze results:** Compare configurations and identify trade-offs.

**Sampling and statistical techniques:**

Because full benchmark simulations are slow (hours to days per benchmark), architects use sampling techniques:
- **SimPoint:** Identifies representative phases of a program and simulates only those phases. Reduces simulation time by 1000× while maintaining accuracy.
- **SmartSim:** Uses machine learning to predict performance based on a small number of simulations.
- **Regression models:** Fit a mathematical model to the simulation data and use it to predict performance for untested configurations.

**Pareto-optimal designs:**

A design is Pareto-optimal if no other design is better in all metrics. For example, if design A is faster than design B but consumes more power, both may be Pareto-optimal (depending on the trade-off). The set of Pareto-optimal designs forms the "Pareto frontier," which represents the best trade-offs between metrics.

**Machine learning for design space exploration:**

Recent research uses machine learning to accelerate design space exploration:
- **Surrogate models:** Train a neural network or Gaussian process on a small set of simulations to predict performance for other configurations.
- **Bayesian optimization:** Iteratively select configurations to simulate based on the model's uncertainty, focusing on promising regions.
- **Reinforcement learning:** Train an agent to explore the design space and find optimal configurations.

These techniques can reduce the number of simulations needed by 10–100×.

screens.title: Design Space Exploration
screens.subtitle: Systematically finding processor designs that balance performance, power, and area

narration.text: Design space exploration is the disciplined process of evaluating many processor configurations to meet constraints such as performance, power, and area. You will learn what the design space includes, why exhaustive search is infeasible, and how simulation, statistical sampling, and machine learning help you find good designs efficiently. A typical design space includes parameters like pipeline depth, issue width, cache sizes and associativity, ROB size, branch predictor capacity, functional units, and memory bandwidth. Together these parameters create millions of possible configurations, so architects use simulators such as Gem5 for detailed study and faster tools like Sniper for broad sweeps. In this lesson you will see how to structure exploration: pick representative benchmarks, define metrics such as IPC and energy, run sampled simulations, and analyze results for Pareto-optimality. We will also show hands-on guidance for changing cache sizes and issue width in Gem5 and how to interpret trade-offs. By the end you should be able to explain why SimPoint sampling matters, how surrogate models reduce simulation cost, and how to read a Pareto frontier to make design decisions. Consider: which metric matters most for the product you care about?

keyIdea.title: Why DSE matters
keyIdea.text: It finds practical processor designs by exploring parameter trade-offs with simulation, sampling, and machine learning.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain what design space exploration is and why it is necessary for modern processor design. You will learn to set up simulations to evaluate microarchitectural parameters such as pipeline depth, issue width, and cache sizes, and to interpret metrics like IPC, energy, and area. You will practice using sampling methods so that you can run far fewer simulations while keeping accurate comparisons, and you will understand what makes a design Pareto-optimal so you can identify useful trade-offs. Finally, you will gain familiarity with common simulators — Gem5, SimpleScalar, Sniper, ZSim, and Marss-x86 — and know when to use a detailed versus a fast simulator. Each objective pairs a practical skill with why it matters: faster exploration saves time and money, better metrics sharpen decisions, and knowing a Pareto frontier prevents chasing dominated designs. These skills let you evaluate real-world variants and communicate trade-offs to stakeholders. Imagine choosing the one metric that most affects your product and using these skills to justify that choice.

narration.text: These practical objectives translate theory into hands-on capability. You will learn to pick representative benchmarks such as SPEC C P U or a matrix multiplication kernel and to define the metrics that matter for your goals: IPC for raw throughput, watts or joules for power and energy, and area proxies such as cache bytes and issue-width-related structures. You will design a small experiment: a base configuration and several variants that double a cache level or increase issue width, then run the benchmark and compare IPC and execution time. You will learn to compute relative speedup and to normalize performance by area when area is proportional to cache size and issue width. Assessment asks you to explain why SimPoint is essential and to produce a short Pareto plot showing which designs are non-dominated. The practical rhythm is: configure, run sampled simulations, collect metrics, fit simple regression or surrogate models if needed, and interpret the Pareto frontier. These lab skills let you turn architectural intuition into measured evidence.

screens.title: What is Design Space Exploration?
screens.subtitle: Definition, scope, and why exhaustive search is impractical

narration.text: Design space exploration is the systematic evaluation of microarchitectural configurations to find designs that meet goals like high performance, low power, or small area. It treats parameters—pipeline depth, issue width, caches, ROB entries, branch predictor capacity, number of functional units, and memory bandwidth—as dimensions in a large space. The chapter gives concrete ranges: pipeline depth from 5 to 20 stages, issue width from 1 to 8, cache sizes from 8 KB to 64 MB, associativity up to 32 ways, ROB sizes between 40 and 900 entries, branch predictor sizes from 1K to 64K entries, and memory bandwidth spanning 10 to 1000 gigabytes per second. These ranges multiply quickly: for example, ten parameters with five options each produce 5^10, or 9,765,625, possible configurations. Because exhaustive evaluation is impossible, architects define constraints and prioritize regions to explore. A common misconception is to treat the space as uniform; in reality some parameters interact strongly — doubling an L1 may matter little if the working set fits in L2, and increasing issue width yields diminishing returns if instruction-level parallelism is limited. The concrete claim is: DSE is about structured sampling and measurement, not brute force. Reflect: which parameter interactions would you prioritize for your workload?

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: DSE systematically searches a high-dimensional parameter space to find practical trade-offs; it relies on sampling because exhaustive search is infeasible.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › What is Design Space Exploration?
Definition & scope

Design space exploration evaluates combinations of microarchitectural parameters to identify designs that satisfy constraints. The space includes both structural choices and microarchitectural buffer sizes, and interactions among parameters determine where improvements are possible.

Parameter ranges (examples):
  • Pipeline depth: 5–20 stages
  • Issue width: 1–8 instructions per cycle
  • Cache size: 8 KB–64 MB; associativity: 1–32 way
  • ROB size: 40–900 entries; branch predictor: 1K–64K entries
Common misconception
Changing a single parameter always helps. In practice, effects depend on other parameters and workload characteristics.
Why exhaustive search fails

Combinatorial growth means millions of configurations even with modest option counts. Evaluating each configuration with full benchmarks would take impractical time. The goal is to find good regions using sampling and models rather than brute force.

Concrete example
With 10 parameters and 5 choices each, you have 5^10 = 9,765,625 configurations. Sampling or surrogate models typically reduce the number of required full simulations by orders of magnitude.
Key Takeaway
Focus exploration on interacting parameters and use sampling to find candidate designs efficiently.

screens.title: Core Design Parameters and Their Effects
screens.subtitle: How pipeline depth, issue width, caches, ROB size and bandwidth shape behavior

narration.text: Architectural parameters each influence performance, power, and area in characteristic ways, and understanding these effects guides sensible exploration. Pipeline depth often trades clock frequency potential against branch misprediction and pipeline flush cost; deeper pipelines can reach higher frequency but may hurt IPC when branch penalties dominate. Issue width increases potential instruction-level parallelism but yields diminishing returns when a workload lacks parallelism; it also increases area for issue logic and functional units. Cache sizes and associativity directly affect miss rates; larger caches reduce misses but cost area and power. ROB size controls the window of in-flight instructions and can improve IPC when it allows more out-of-order execution, but large ROBs increase area and wakeup complexity. Memory bandwidth caps achievable throughput for memory-bound workloads; increasing bandwidth benefits those workloads but adds cost. A common example: doubling L1 may help workloads with small working sets but gives little benefit when most misses are resolved in L2. A misconception is to assume parameters are independent; in practice, increasing issue width without sufficient ROB or instruction supply yields little benefit. When you design experiments, pick parameters whose interactions are likely to matter for your target workload.

keyIdea.title: Parameter interactions
keyIdea.text: Parameters influence each other; prioritize exploring parameters whose interaction is likely to affect your workload's bottlenecks.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › Core Design Parameters
Parameter hierarchy
Pipeline depth (5–20)
Affects clock potential and branch penalty; deeper pipelines may improve frequency but increase misprediction cost.
Issue width (1–8)
More parallelism capacity but higher area and diminishing returns without parallelism in code.
Cache sizes & associativity (8 KB–64 MB, 1–32 way)
Larger caches reduce misses; associativity reduces conflict misses at area cost.
Buffers and bandwidth
ROB size (40–900)
Larger ROB increases instruction window for out-of-order execution, improving IPC until diminishing returns.
Branch predictor (1K–64K)
Larger predictors reduce mispredictions but add area and power.
Memory bandwidth (10–1000 GB/s)
Caps throughput for memory-bound workloads; adding bandwidth helps those workloads but increases cost.
Key Takeaway

Choose parameters to explore based on likely bottlenecks and the interactions that affect your workload's behavior.

screens.title: Combinatorial Explosion and Search Strategy
screens.subtitle: Why search needs to be selective and how to narrow the space

narration.text: The design space grows combinatorially as you add parameters and options, so a direct exhaustive search is usually impossible. The chapter gives a clear numeric example: ten parameters with five choices each yield nearly ten million configurations. Running full benchmark simulations across that many points would take years. To manage this, architects adopt selective search strategies: prune unlikely regions using domain knowledge, focus on parameters that influence your workload, and use sampling or surrogate models to predict unseen points. A useful misconception check is to avoid random blind sampling for parameters that have strong interactions; instead, combine targeted sampling with statistical techniques. Practical search strategies include Latin hypercube or factorial sampling to cover the space more evenly, but the chapter emphasizes simulation-driven approaches: SimPoint identifies representative program phases, and tools like SmartSim or regression models predict performance from a few measured points. When building an exploration plan, include a baseline, a small set of informed variants, and a staged approach where fast simulators explore broadly and detailed simulators validate promising candidates. Ask yourself: where will you apply detailed simulation versus fast approximate models?

keyIdea.title: Search strategy
keyIdea.text: Combine domain knowledge, targeted sampling, and models to find high-value regions without exhaustively evaluating the entire space.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › Combinatorial Explosion
Why exhaustive search fails

Even moderate parameter counts create millions of configs. Full simulations for each point are slow. The practical response is to narrow the search with informed sampling and modeling.

Strategy checklist
  • Use domain knowledge to prune irrelevant parameters.
  • Run fast simulators to scan broadly, detailed simulators to validate.
  • Apply sampling and surrogate models to predict untested points.
Example workflow
1. Define baseline and a small, informed set of variants. 2. Use a fast simulator or sampling method to explore many variants. 3. Fit a surrogate or regression model to measured results. 4. Validate promising points with a detailed simulator like Gem5.
Common mistake
Relying on a single simulator or sampling plan without validation. Fast models need targeted detailed runs to confirm predictions.

screens.title: Architectural Simulators: Trade-offs
screens.subtitle: Comparing Gem5, SimpleScalar, Sniper, ZSim, and Marss-x86

narration.text: Simulation tools are the microscope of design space exploration. The chapter highlights several simulators and their roles. SimpleScalar is an early configurable simulator modeling a MIPS-like pipeline and remains useful for basic experiments. Gem5 is described as the current academic standard, with support for x86, ARM, and RISC-V, detailed cache, memory, and interconnect models, and modes for full-system or syscall-emulation. Sniper and ZSim are faster alternatives: Sniper uses interval modeling for speed, and ZSim leverages parallel techniques; both enable broader sweeps when cycle-by-cycle detail is too costly. Marss-x86 provides detailed x86 simulation based on PTLSim. Choose tools based on the trade-off between accuracy and throughput: use Gem5 to validate detailed microarchitectural interactions where correctness matters and Sniper or ZSim when you need to screen many configurations quickly. A common misunderstanding is to expect identical numbers from different simulators; instead, treat fast simulators as comparative tools for trends and use detailed models to confirm final choices. When planning an exploration, assign simulators to stages: broad sweep with fast tools, targeted validation with Gem5, and cross-checks for corner cases. Architectural Simulators: Trade-offs means use fast simulators for broad sweeps and gem5 or marss-x86 for detailed validation; understand each tool's accuracy vs. speed trade-off.. In practical terms, comparing gem5, simplescalar, sniper, zsim, and marss-x86. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Simulator roles
keyIdea.text: Use fast simulators for broad sweeps and Gem5 or Marss-x86 for detailed validation; understand each tool's accuracy vs. speed trade-off.

Practical tip
Plan your exploration stages: fast simulators for wide scans, detailed simulators for final validation and corner cases.

screens.title: Simulation Methodology
screens.subtitle: Benchmarks, metrics, configuration, execution, and analysis

narration.text: A reliable simulation methodology follows a clear sequence: select benchmarks that represent your workload, choose metrics to measure, configure the simulator, run simulations, and analyze results. First, pick representative workloads such as SPEC C P U, PARSEC, or targeted kernels like matrix multiplication; representative workloads ensure the results generalize. Second, decide metrics: IPC is the primary performance metric, while power (watts), energy (joules), and area (mm² or proxies) complete the picture. Third, configure the simulator: set clock rate, issue width, cache sizes, ROB entries, and other parameters. The chapter's hands-on activity uses a 2 GHz baseline with 4-issue, 128-entry ROB, and a cache hierarchy of 32 KB L1, 256 KB L2, and 8 MB L3. Fourth, run simulations and collect statistics. Because full runs can be slow, combine sampling techniques with careful configuration to limit time. Finally, analyze data: compare IPC and execution time across variants, compute normalized speedups, and plot trade-offs. A common pitfall is to compare raw IPC without normalizing for area or power when those are design constraints. End by asking: does this metric set let you choose a practical candidate under your constraints?

keyIdea.title: Method checklist
keyIdea.text: Follow benchmark selection, metric definition, careful configuration, sampled execution, and analysis to produce defensible comparisons.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › Simulation Methodology
Five-step process
1. Select benchmarks
Pick representative suites like SPEC CPU, PARSEC, or focused kernels to exercise the microarchitecture.
2. Choose metrics
IPC, power, energy, and area proxies. Decide which metric is primary and which are constraints.
3. Configure simulator
Set clock, issue width, ROB size, cache sizes and other parameters for baseline and variants.
4. Run simulations
Use sampling to reduce time; run full detailed simulations for validation points.
5. Analyze results
Compute speedups, normalize by area or energy, and identify Pareto-optimal designs.
Concrete baseline used in the lab
Base: 2 GHz, 4-issue, 128-entry ROB, 32 KB L1, 256 KB L2, 8 MB L3. Variants adjust cache sizes or issue width, then measure IPC and execution time to compute speedup and speedup-per-area.
Pitfall
Comparing raw IPC without accounting for area or power can mislead decisions when those are constraints.

screens.title: Sampling Techniques: SimPoint, SmartSim, Regression
screens.subtitle: How sampling reduces simulation cost while preserving accuracy

narration.text: Because full benchmark simulations can take hours or days per configuration, sampling techniques let architects simulate only a small fraction of execution while preserving accuracy. SimPoint identifies representative phases of program execution by analyzing basic block vectors and clustering similar behavior; it selects a few simulation points and simulates only those short ranges, reducing runtime by roughly three orders of magnitude while maintaining high accuracy. SmartSim takes a machine learning approach and predicts performance from a limited set of simulations. Regression models or simpler surrogate models fit a mathematical function to measured data and predict performance for untested configurations. A common misconception is to assume sampling always reduces accuracy substantially; in practice, methods like SimPoint maintain low error — the chapter notes less than 3% error compared to full simulation in published results. When you use sampling, choose representative benchmarks, validate the sampled points against a few full runs, and be cautious about phase changes introduced by parameter changes. Sampling is most reliable when program phases are stable across configurations. Ask: which workloads in your target set are most phase-stable and thus amenable to SimPoint?

keyIdea.title: Sampling value
keyIdea.text: Sampling such as SimPoint can reduce simulation time by ~1000× while keeping accuracy; validate sampled results with a few detailed runs.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › Sampling & Statistics
SimPoint (phase sampling)
SimPoint finds representative program phases via basic block vectors. It clusters execution behavior and selects short simulation points that represent the whole run. This reduces runtime dramatically while preserving accuracy; published studies report less than 3% error in many cases.
When to use
Programs with stable phases across configurations; validate with some full runs.
SmartSim & regression
SmartSim uses machine learning to predict performance from a small set of simulations. Regression and surrogate models fit functions to data and estimate performance for untested points. These methods can reduce simulations by 10–100× depending on model quality.
Practical tip
Always reserve a few validation runs to measure the surrogate model's error before trusting predictions.

screens.title: Pareto-optimal Designs and Trade-offs
screens.subtitle: Interpreting the Pareto frontier to make decisions

narration.text: A Pareto-optimal design is one that is not dominated by any other across the chosen metrics. Dominance means another design is at least as good in every metric and strictly better in one. When metrics conflict, such as higher performance versus lower power, multiple Pareto-optimal designs can exist. The Pareto frontier is the set of these non-dominated designs and visualizes the best trade-offs available. Use it to narrow choices: once you plot designs by two axes, such as IPC versus power, the frontier shows the ridge of most efficient trade-offs. A practical example: design A gives higher IPC but consumes more power than design B; both are Pareto-optimal if neither dominates the other on both metrics. The frontier thereby eliminates dominated designs and focuses stakeholder discussion. Misconceptions include treating the frontier as a single 'best' point — instead, the final choice depends on constraints and priorities. To apply this, compute IPC and energy or area proxies for each variant, plot the points, and identify the frontier. Ask: which designs on the frontier fit your power or area budget? Pareto-optimal Designs and Trade-offs means the pareto frontier shows non-dominated designs and helps focus decisions where metrics conflict; selection requires external priorities or constraints.. In practical terms, interpreting the pareto frontier to make decisions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pareto frontier
keyIdea.text: The Pareto frontier shows non-dominated designs and helps focus decisions where metrics conflict; selection requires external priorities or constraints.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › Pareto-optimal Designs
Pareto explanation

A design is Pareto-optimal if no other design is better in every metric. The Pareto frontier is the set of such designs and represents the best trade-offs among chosen objectives, for example IPC versus power or IPC versus area.

Usage pattern
  • Compute metrics for variants.
  • Plot designs in metric space and identify the non-dominated ridge.
  • Choose a point on the frontier that meets constraints or stakeholder priorities.
Concrete contrast
If A is faster but uses more power than B, and neither dominates the other across metrics, both can sit on the Pareto frontier. Designs not on the frontier are strictly inferior and can be discarded from consideration.
Key Takeaway
Use the frontier to reduce options to the most efficient trade-offs; choose among them based on external constraints.

screens.title: Machine Learning for Design Space Exploration
screens.subtitle: Surrogate models, Bayesian optimization, and reinforcement learning

narration.text: Machine learning accelerates exploration by predicting performance or selecting promising configurations. Surrogate models — neural networks or Gaussian processes — are trained on a small set of simulation results to predict performance metrics for untested points. This reduces the number of expensive simulations by enabling quick evaluations across the space. Bayesian optimization uses the surrogate's uncertainty to guide sampling, iteratively selecting points that are likely to improve the objective or reduce uncertainty; it focuses simulation budget where it matters most. Reinforcement learning frames exploration as a sequential decision problem where an agent chooses configurations and learns policies that find high-performing designs efficiently. The chapter reports that ML techniques can reduce the number of required simulations by 10–100× in many scenarios. Practical cautions: models generalize only within the distribution of training points, so poor coverage leads to bad predictions; always validate model predictions with targeted simulations. A concrete approach is to use a small, diverse training set, fit a surrogate, apply Bayesian optimization to propose candidates, and validate the best ones with detailed simulation. Consider: which ML approach fits your budget and available simulation data?

keyIdea.title: ML accelerators
keyIdea.text: Surrogates and Bayesian optimization can dramatically reduce simulation needs, but require careful validation and representative training data.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › Machine Learning for DSE
Surrogate models

Train a neural network or Gaussian process on a limited set of simulation results to predict IPC, power, or other metrics for untested configurations. Surrogates are fast to evaluate and enable broad searches.

Best practice
  • Use a diverse training set that covers the intended search region.
  • Hold out validation points and use them to estimate model error before trusting predictions.
Bayesian optimization & RL

Bayesian optimization uses uncertainty to pick informative samples; reinforcement learning frames search as sequential decision-making and can learn policies that find good designs quickly.

Warning
Models extrapolate poorly outside the training distribution. Validate candidate predictions with detailed simulations before committing to design changes.

screens.title: Hands-on: Gem5 Variant Experiments
screens.subtitle: Run baseline and cache/issue-width variants; measure IPC and execution time

narration.text: The hands-on activity uses Gem5 or a pre-built binary to compare variants derived from a base configuration. The base is: 2 GHz, 4-issue, 128-entry ROB, 32 KB L1, 256 KB L2, and an 8 MB L3. Variants double L1, L2, or L3 individually, and one variant increases issue width to 8. The practical steps are: 1) set up the simulator to run a simple benchmark like matrix multiplication or a SPEC C P U test; 2) run the baseline with sampling or a short SimPoint interval if available; 3) run each variant and collect IPC and execution time; 4) compute relative speedup and normalize by area, assuming area is proportional to cache size and issue width. If you cannot run Gem5, simulate the analysis mentally using the known effects: doubling L1 should help workloads with working sets near L1 size, doubling L2 helps medium working sets, and increasing issue width helps only when instruction-level parallelism exists. A common mistake is to change multiple parameters at once without isolating effects. End by asking: which variant gives the best speedup per unit area for your workload and why?

keyIdea.title: Lab focus
keyIdea.text: Run baseline and isolated variants in Gem5, collect IPC/time, and compute speedup-per-area while validating sampling assumptions.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › Hands-on: Gem5 Variant Experiments
Experiment plan
  • Baseline: 2 GHz, 4-issue, 128 ROB, 32 KB L1, 256 KB L2, 8 MB L3.
  • Variant A: L1 = 64 KB. Variant B: L2 = 512 KB. Variant C: L3 = 16 MB. Variant D: issue width = 8.
  • Run benchmark, collect IPC and execution time, compute speedups and speedup-per-area.
Minimal command example
# Example invocation (conceptual)
# Configure baseline and run a short benchmark or SimPoint interval
build/gem5.opt configs/example/se.py --cpu-type=O3_CPU --num-cpus=1 \
  --clock=2GHz --issue-width=4 --rob-size=128 \
  --l1-size=32kB --l2-size=256kB --l3-size=8MB \
  --cmd=matrix_mul

# Repeat with variants by changing l1-size, l2-size, l3-size, or issue-width
Analysis card
Compute speedup = baseline_time / variant_time, and speedup-per-area = speedup / (relative area). Assume area proportional to cache bytes and issue-width when comparing variants. Use plots or a small table to find Pareto-optimal candidates.
Pro-tip
Isolate one parameter per variant so you can attribute performance changes reliably; validate sampling assumptions with at least one full run per benchmark.

screens.title: Metrics and Trade-off Calculations
screens.subtitle: IPC, power, energy, area proxies, and how to compute speedup-per-area

narration.text: Choosing metrics and calculating normalized trade-offs lets you compare designs fairly. IPC measures instruction throughput and is the primary performance indicator; execution time complements IPC when clock frequency varies. Power (watts) and energy (joules) measure instantaneous and cumulative cost; area is often represented by mm² or a proxy proportional to cache bytes and issue-width related structures. The hands-on lab suggests using area proportional to cache sizes and issue width for a rough comparison. To compute speedup-per-area: first compute speedup as baseline_time divided by variant_time, or equivalently variant_IPC divided by baseline_IPC when clocks are equal. Next compute the relative area factor: for example, if you double L1 size, area factor might be 2× for the cache portion; combine cache and structure contributions to get total relative area. Finally divide speedup by the relative area to rank variants by performance per unit area. A misconception is to treat area as precisely proportional to cache bytes; while a useful proxy, real area models are more nuanced. Always state your area assumptions when presenting results. End with a question: which normalization will most affect your ranking if area estimates change?

keyIdea.title: Normalization
keyIdea.text: Normalize performance by area or energy when constraints matter; state assumptions and validate sensitivity to those assumptions.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.6 › Metrics & Trade-offs
Key metrics
  • IPC — instructions per cycle, primary performance metric.
  • Execution time — wall-clock time for a workload, complements IPC.
  • Power and energy — watts and joules for runtime cost.
  • Area — use proxies like cache bytes and issue-width related area for quick comparisons.
Speedup-per-area example
If baseline_time = 100s and variant_time = 80s, speedup = 100/80 = 1.25. If variant doubles L1 (area factor 1.2 overall when combined with other structures), then speedup-per-area = 1.25 / 1.2 ≈ 1.04. Rank variants by this metric to evaluate performance efficiency under area constraints.
Caveat
Area proxies are approximations. If precise area matters, use detailed layout or synthesis estimates to refine comparisons.

screens.title: Key Concepts
screens.subtitle: What to remember from this chapter

narration.text: Keep three core ideas in mind. First, the design space is high-dimensional and grows combinatorially; you cannot evaluate every point, so prioritize and sample carefully. Second, simulation tools have different roles: Gem5 and Marss-x86 give detailed, cycle-accurate validation while Sniper and ZSim enable broader, faster sweeps. Third, sampling, surrogate models, and Bayesian optimization dramatically cut the number of simulations needed; validate model predictions with targeted detailed runs to avoid surprises. Also remember the Pareto frontier: it focuses decisions on non-dominated trade-offs between metrics like IPC, power, and area. When you run experiments, isolate parameters in variants, normalize metrics when appropriate, and state your area or energy assumptions. These practices let you turn architectural hypotheses into measurable evidence. Ask yourself after each experiment: have I validated sampling assumptions and checked that my surrogate predictions hold for the most promising points?

keyIdea.title: Essential takeaway
keyIdea.text: Use sampling and modeling to explore efficiently, choose the right simulator for the stage, and rely on Pareto analysis to make trade-offs clear.

narration.text: Remember three compact reminders: first, define clear metrics and a baseline before you change parameters. Second, match your simulator to the stage of exploration — use fast tools for broad scans, detailed tools for validation. Third, use sampling and surrogate models to reduce simulation count, but always validate the model's predictions with detailed runs on promising designs. These rules keep exploration practical and results defensible. When presenting results, show the Pareto frontier and state your area and energy assumptions so stakeholders can choose according to real constraints. Finally, treat parameter interactions as the primary source of surprise; design experiments that isolate effects and measure sensitivity. With these practices you can turn architectural choices into measurable, communicable trade-offs.
